title: Incomplete Harm Severity Taxonomy + Regulatory Reliance: Governance Failure Compounding

original_idea.title: Incomplete Harm Severity Taxonomy + Regulatory Reliance: Governance Failure Compounding
original_idea.problem: Only 14/210 benchmarks provide principled harm severity justification. If regulators rely on these same benchmarks for pass/fail certification, the compound failure is: ad hoc severity thresholds create false institutional oversight.
original_idea.direction: Map the harm severity taxonomies used in the 14 principled benchmarks against regulatory risk frameworks (EU AI Act risk categories, NIST AI RMF). Identify misalignments. Propose a harm severity taxonomy anchored to regulatory risk categories.
original_idea.why_it_matters: The direct link between benchmark quality and regulatory legitimacy creates a compounding governance failure when benchmark severity taxonomies are unjustified.
original_idea.relevant_context: The 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' arxiv paper specifically analyzes the 210 benchmark survey. The EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF provide regulatory anchor points.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: bridging benchmark taxonomies to regulatory frameworks directly improves governance validity. Each link from taxonomy mapping to policy improvement is explicit.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Taxonomy mapping and gap analysis is analytical work requiring reading and classification, not ML. Accessible to CS students with guidance on regulatory frameworks.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Mapping 14 benchmarks against two regulatory frameworks and proposing a new taxonomy is broad. Could be scoped to 3-4 benchmarks and one framework for 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: AI risk taxonomies exist (MIT AI Risk Repository with 1,612 classified risks; various safety risk taxonomies). The EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF frameworks are well-documented. Cross-framework mapping guides exist (EC Council, CSA). However, the specific exercise of mapping the 14 principled harm severity taxonomies from the 210-benchmark survey against regulatory risk frameworks -- identifying misalignments and proposing a regulatory-anchored severity taxonomy -- is mostly novel. The bridge between benchmark-level severity justification and regulatory risk categories has not been systematically built.
